annotator.notes: Student incorrectly assumes all numbers have an even number of divisors; tutor guides them to discover perfect squares.

task_context.problem_statement: Write a python function to check whether the count of divisors is even. https://www.w3resource.com/python-exercises/basic/python-basic-1-exercise-24.php

messages.content: I'm stuck on this assignment: Write a python function to check whether the count of divisors is even. https://www.w3resource.com/python-exercises/basic/python-basic-1-exercise-24.php. Can you just give me the code? I'm in a rush.
I can't provide the full code for you, but I can definitely help you build it step-by-step! To get started, how would you normally find all the divisors of a number if you were doing it on paper?

I'd just list the pairs. Like for 12, it's 1&12, 2&6, 3&4. That's 6 divisors, which is even. Actually, wait—don't all numbers have an even number of divisors because they always come in pairs? If that's true, the function should just return True for everything.
That is a very logical observation! Most divisors do come in pairs. However, try testing that theory with a few different numbers. What happens if you look at a number like 9 or 16?
Let's see... for 9, the divisors are 1, 3, and 9. That's 3 divisors. Oh! 3 is odd. So the 'pairs' rule breaks when the number is a perfect square because the square root pairs with itself.

Exactly. You've found the exception. Now that we know some numbers have an odd count of divisors, how could you translate this into a Python function? You could either count all the divisors or use a mathematical property of the numbers we just discussed.
I'll try counting them. I can use a for loop from 1 to n and check if n % i == 0. But that might be slow for huge numbers. Is there a faster way to loop?

You're thinking about efficiency, which is great. Remember how you mentioned divisors come in pairs? If you find one divisor 'i', you automatically know that 'n / i' is also a divisor. Based on that, do you think you need to loop all the way up to 'n'?
